newsitem.title: USA: Continental, pilots set to begin talks.
newsitem.headline: Continental, pilots set to begin talks.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc, the fifth-largest U.S. airline, and its pilots will begin contract talks next week that will likely result in a sizable pay increase for union members, analysts said.
"Continental's pilots are starting from very far behind. There is ample room for negotiations there," said Timothy Ross, an analyst with SBC Warburg.
Houston-based Continental is one of several U.S.-based airlines to face contract talks with its pilots this year.
UAL Corp's United Airlines recently reached a tentative mid-term wage pact with its pilots, after they rejected an earlier agreement.

AMR Corp's labor woes remain unresolved. Pilots at its American Airlines have not yet decided whether to accept the latest contract proposal. US Airways Group Inc, meanwhile, is seeking pay cuts for its pilots.

Continental's pilots union said its 4,900 members currently earn about 35 percent less than their peers at rival airlines because of wage concessions made in 1992 to help the company through its financial difficulties. The pilots said they have only been partially compensated for $38 million in concessions.

"We're the No.1 airline in the industry as far as performance. There are a lot of positives at the airline, and we want some parity with others in the industry," said Leonard Nikolia, president of the Independent Association of Continental Pilots.
The pilots union said it was open to discussing profit-sharing or taking an equity stake in the company, though it insisted that the talks stay focused on wage increases.
"There's no straight (wage) demand. We just hope to recapture our earnings potential," said Bill Borrelli, a vice president with the pilots union.
The union said its board would meet Wednesday and Thursday to plan its strategy ahead of the April meetings with management.

The pilots are making their demands at a time of prosperity for Continental. Since emerging from its second bankruptcy four years ago, Continental has repaired its balance sheet, improved its hub operations and added international alliance partners.
The carrier posted record profits in 1996, earning $319 million on revenues of $6.4 billion, up from $224 million in profits on revenues of $5.8 billion the previous year.
Continental recently said it expected to beat Wall Street's first-quarter consensus earnings estimate of $0.72 a share.
When contract negotiations begin April 1, the tone is likely to be less contentious than the atmosphere at the American Airlines talks, analysts said.

American's pilots went on strike briefly in February before being sent back to work by a Presidential Emergency Board set up by President Bill Clinton. American and its pilots are attempting to reach a compromise. A 60-day cooling off period, which prevents a strike or a lock-out, is currently in effect.
"Unlike American, we don't have an adversarial relationship with management," Nikolia said.

The almost cordial relationship seen recently between Continental and its employees contrasts sharply with the past. Labor relations were more hostile under the tenure of former Chairman Frank Lorenzo, who put Continental into bankruptcy in 1983 and rescinded its labor agreements.
The pilots have applauded current Chairman Gordon Bethune's turnaround efforts.
"The pilots will be economically very demanding, but they will be reasonable." said Candace Browning, an analyst with Merrill Lynch said.

"They've seen their airline go through some very rocky times, so they don't want to see any damaged done to the company," Browning said. "There are going to be tough negotiations, but nothing really ugly like a strike," she said.
Continental's management is expected to be more receptive to the pilot's demands than other carriers have been during recent labor talks, analysts said.

"Management is of a mind to increase wages, but within reason," said Edward Starkman, an analyst with Dillon Read. Starkman expects the pilots to win some wage increases, but their pay is expected to remain less than the industry average.
Continental's Bethune previously said he expected to reach an agreement that provides increased pay for the pilots.
"Pilots deserve what's fair for the pilots. ... I see no reason to have acrimony, disruption and heartburn," Bethune said previously.

Indeed, the carrier has already shared some of its good fortune with its employees. In February, on the eve of American's brief strike, Continental distributed $68 million in profit-sharing checks to its staff.
Continental's festivities were more than a just a calculated public relations stunt, analysts said.
"It's symbolic of the attitude of top management of company. They're trying on all levels to empower employees," Browning said.
((--New York newsdesk, 212-859-1610))
